ask.conflicts.what-conflict-is.prompt: In your own words: what has actually gone wrong when git reports a conflict?
ask.conflicts.what-conflict-is.modelAnsw: Nothing is broken. Two branches edited the same lines, and git will not pick one for me, because picking would mean throwing away somebody’s work on a guess. It merges different parts of a file without asking; it stops only where the changes overlap. It is a question, not an error.

step.javascript.title: The JavaScript this project assumes
quiz.javascript.what-import-does.prompt: A file has `export function parsePriceCents(...)`. Another has `import { parsePriceCents } from '@/lib/products'`. What is the `export` for?
It makes the function public on the internet.
Nothing outside a file can see anything in it unless the file offers it.
It is required on every function in TypeScript.
It runs the function when the file loads.
quiz.javascript.what-import-does.explain: A file is a sealed box. `export` is the file offering something outward; `import` is another file asking for it by name. That is why the failing test in a few steps says "Failed to resolve import" — you will be importing from a file that does not exist yet.
quiz.javascript.destructure.option.a: Copies the whole of `body` into a variable called `data`.
quiz.javascript.destructure.option.b: Pulls the `data` property out of `body` into its own variable.
quiz.javascript.destructure.option.c: Creates a new object containing only `data`.
quiz.javascript.destructure.explain: It is shorthand for `const data = body.data;`. The braces are a pattern describing the shape you want out. `const [posts, setPosts] = useState(...)` is the same idea with square brackets, for arrays — which is why the two things `useState` gives back can be named whatever you like.
step.requests.title: Watch the conversation
check.requests.app-up: The app is running, so you can make requests to it
quiz.requests.html-vs-json.prompt: You asked for `/posts` and then `/api/posts`. What was different about what came back?
quiz.requests.html-vs-json.option.a: Nothing — they returned the same thing.
quiz.requests.html-vs-json.option.b: `/posts` returned HTML for a browser to draw; `/api/posts` returned JSON data.
quiz.requests.html-vs-json.explain: Same information, two audiences. A page is dressed up for a person — headings, layout, styling. An API answers with the values themselves, because the thing reading it is a program. That is the entire difference, and you just watched it.
quiz.requests.empty-post.prompt: You sent a `POST` to `/api/posts` with an empty body. What status code came back?
quiz.requests.empty-post.explain: 400 — "I cannot make sense of what you sent". The handler checked the body before touching the database and refused it politely. Note what it did *not* do: crash, or claim success. You will write that check yourself in a few steps.
quiz.requests.missing-path.prompt: And `curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/nope` gave you which status?
quiz.requests.missing-path.explain: 404 — the server answered perfectly well, there is just nothing at that address. That is worth separating in your head from "the server is down", which gives you no response at all, and from 500, which means it broke while trying.
ask.requests.get-repeat.prompt: You ran the same `GET` three times and got the same answer, having changed nothing. Why does it matter that a GET behaves that way?
ask.requests.get-repeat.modelAnswer: Because a GET gets repeated by things that never asked me. Pressing back, refreshing, a search engine following a link — all re-issue it. That is only safe because a GET is meant to read and not change. Anything that does change something has to be a POST, which is why the create form on `/posts` is one.
ask.requests.get-repeat.lookFor.0: browsers, caches and crawlers repeat GETs without asking
ask.requests.get-repeat.lookFor.1: a GET that changed things would change them unpredictably
ask.requests.get-repeat.lookFor.2: that is why the create form sends a POST instead
step.two-machines.title: Which machine is this running on?
check.two-machines.server-log: You added a log to the page
check.two-machines.browser-log: You added a log to the component
attest.two-machines.saw-split.label: I saw `[server]` in the container log and `[browser]` in the browser console
attest.two-machines.saw-split.hint: Two different places, and neither message appeared in the other.
attest.two-machines.found-source.label: I found `posts-board.tsx` in the browser’s Sources tab
quiz.two-machines.where-logged.prompt: Why did `[server]` appear in the container log and `[browser]` in the browser console?
quiz.two-machines.where-logged.option.a: Next.js routes server logs to the terminal for tidiness.
quiz.two-machines.where-logged.option.b: They ran on two different computers — one on the server, one on the machine in front of you.
quiz.two-machines.where-logged.option.c: The browser console hides some messages.
quiz.two-machines.where-logged.explain: A `console.log` prints wherever it runs. Nothing was routed or hidden — the two files genuinely executed on two machines.
quiz.two-machines.why-secret.prompt: You found your component’s source in the browser. What follows from that?
quiz.two-machines.why-secret.option.a: Nothing — only developers can see it.
quiz.two-machines.why-secret.option.b: That file cannot hold a password or an API key, because everyone using the app has a copy.
quiz.two-machines.why-secret.option.c: You should minify it before shipping.
quiz.two-machines.why-secret.option.d: The browser copied it by mistake.
quiz.two-machines.why-secret.explain: Anything sent to a browser belongs to whoever owns that browser. Minifying changes nothing. So secrets stay in server code — and a component in the browser that needs data has to ask the server for it.
ask.two-machines.why-two-places.prompt: In your own words: why did one `console.log` print in the terminal and the other in the browser?
ask.two-machines.why-two-places.modelAns: They ran in different places. `page.tsx` ran on the server, so its output went to the server log. `posts-board.tsx` was sent to my browser as code and ran there, so its output went to the browser console. A `console.log` prints wherever the code containing it happens to be running.
the two files ran on different machines
a console.log prints wherever its code is running
the page ran on the server; the component was sent to the browser
step.use-client.title: The line that decides
check.use-client.counter: You added a working counter to the component
check.use-client.use-client-intact: `'use client'` is back on the first line
attest.use-client.removed-marker.label: I removed `'use client'`, read the error, and put it back
attest.use-client.state-on-server.label: I tried `useState` in `page.tsx` and read the error that gave me too
It makes the component load faster.
It sends that component to the browser, so it runs there as well.
It marks the file as belonging to the front end team.
It stops the component being rendered on the server.
quiz.use-client.what-marker-does.explain: It is an instruction about *where the code goes*. Without it, the component runs on the server and only its HTML is sent. With it, the code itself is shipped to the browser — which is what lets it hold state and respond to clicks, and what stops it holding secrets.
ask.use-client.which-to-use.prompt: A filter box that narrows a list as you type needs `'use client'`. A page listing yesterday’s orders does not. What is the difference?
ask.use-client.which-to-use.modelAnswer: The filter has to react to something that happens after the page arrives — my typing — so its code has to be in the browser where the typing is. The orders page is worked out once and then just sits there, so the server can do it with less code and one round trip instead of two. Default to the server; go to the client when something has to respond.
ask.use-client.which-to-use.lookFor.0: the filter changes after the page has loaded, in response to the user
ask.use-client.which-to-use.lookFor.1: the orders page is rendered once and then sits there
ask.use-client.which-to-use.lookFor.2: default to the server and reach for the client when something must react
step.using-ai.title: Using AI without it using you
attest.using-ai.write-not-copy.label: cs50.ai only, and no code enters this repo that I did not write myself
attest.using-ai.write-not-copy.hint: Both halves. Turn off the assistant built into your editor — it suggests as you type, which is the failure mode this step is about. And "write it myself" means read the example, look away, then produce it — not pasted, and not transcribed with the example open.
quiz.using-ai.find-the-bug.prompt: That `newestFirst` function looks right and is wrong twice. Which pair of problems does it have?
quiz.using-ai.find-the-bug.option.a: It sorts oldest-first despite its name, and it reorders the caller’s array in place.
quiz.using-ai.find-the-bug.option.b: It crashes on an empty array, and it is slow.
quiz.using-ai.find-the-bug.option.c: It does not handle `null`, and the return type is wrong.
quiz.using-ai.find-the-bug.explain: `a - b` sorts ascending, which is oldest first — the opposite of the name. And `.sort()` rearranges the array it was given rather than returning a new one, so whoever called it now has their data in a different order without asking. Both are the kind of plausible, confident, wrong code these tools produce, and both are findable by reading it.
quiz.using-ai.good-use.prompt: Which of these can you ask cs50.ai during onboarding without breaking either rule?
quiz.using-ai.good-use.option.a: "Write me a POST endpoint for products."
quiz.using-ai.good-use.option.b: "Here is my endpoint and the error it gives. What should I look at first? Do not fix it."
quiz.using-ai.good-use.option.d: "Write the tests for this so I do not have to."
quiz.using-ai.good-use.explain: It keeps you doing the work. You still have to read the code, form a theory, and make the change — the AI only narrows where to look. The other three hand over the part where the learning happens, and you find out at review, or at the next thing you cannot do.
ask.using-ai.why-type-it.prompt: The rule is not "never look at the examples" — it is read them, look away, then write it. Why the looking away? What would you lose by transcribing it with the example open?
ask.using-ai.why-type-it.modelAnswer: With the example open I am copying, just slowly — I never have to produce anything, because the answer is right there. Looking away turns it into producing, and that is where I discover which lines I could not have written myself, which is the useful information. Transcribing does make me read every character, which is worth something, but afterwards I can only recognise the code rather than write it again.
ask.using-ai.why-type-it.lookFor.0: transcribing is still copying, because the answer is in front of you
ask.using-ai.why-type-it.lookFor.1: producing it from understanding is what makes it stick
ask.using-ai.why-type-it.lookFor.2: you discover which lines you could not have written yourself
ask.using-ai.why-type-it.lookFor.3: afterwards you can write something similar rather than only recognising it
step.decomposition.title: Break the problem down
check.decomposition.sandbox-branch: You are on your sandbox branch
check.decomposition.plan-exists: You wrote your plan down in `PLAN.md`
check.decomposition.plan-tasks: It is a task list, not a paragraph
check.decomposition.plan-ordered: Nothing is built before the thing it needs
quiz.decomposition.two-questions.prompt: "The page needs the endpoint" and "I will build the endpoint on Tuesday" are answers to two different questions. Which pair?
What is hard, and what is easy.
What needs what to exist (dependency), and what order I will work in (sequence).
What the user sees, and what the developer sees.
They are the same question said two ways.
quiz.decomposition.two-questions.explain: Dependency is a fact about the code — the page cannot read from an endpoint that does not exist. Sequence is a choice about your week. They are related, because dependency limits which sequences work, but they are not the same and mixing them up is the commonest way a plan goes wrong.
quiz.decomposition.trace-it.prompt: What is plan tracing, and why bother?
quiz.decomposition.trace-it.option.a: Running the code to see if it works.
quiz.decomposition.trace-it.option.b: Walking through your list in order and asking what actually exists after each line — so you find the gaps before you write anything.
quiz.decomposition.trace-it.option.c: Drawing a diagram of the finished feature.
quiz.decomposition.trace-it.option.d: Asking a senior developer to check your plan.
quiz.decomposition.trace-it.explain: It costs two minutes and finds the two things a plan is usually missing: a step that depends on something not built yet, and a piece nobody remembered at all. Both are far cheaper to find now than on the afternoon you hit them.
ask.decomposition.plan-review.prompt: Paste your task list, then add one sentence: which task did you have the most trouble placing, and what decided it?
ask.decomposition.plan-review.modelAnswe: A good list reads something like: somewhere to keep a product; an address that hands products back; an address that accepts a new one; refusing a bad price; a page that shows them; a form that adds one; a browser test for the whole path. Each is finishable on its own, nothing sits above something that does not exist yet, and reading and writing are separate because they can be finished and checked separately. The hardest to place is usually validation — it is not obviously its own task until you ask who would notice if it were missing.
ask.decomposition.plan-review.lookFor.0: every item is one piece of work, small enough to finish in a sitting
ask.decomposition.plan-review.lookFor.1: nothing appears before the thing it needs to exist
ask.decomposition.plan-review.lookFor.2: reading products and creating one are separate tasks
ask.decomposition.plan-review.lookFor.3: something in the list says how you would know it works
ask.decomposition.plan-review.lookFor.4: the sentence names a real ordering decision rather than restating the list
ask.decomposition.why-storage-first.prom: Why does the storage go first, and the page last? What would go wrong the other way round?
ask.decomposition.why-storage-first.mode: Each layer needs the one below it. The page reads from an address, and that address reads from somewhere the data is kept. If I built the page first there would be nothing real behind it, so I could not tell whether any of it worked — I would be guessing until the very end.
ask.decomposition.why-storage-first.look: each layer needs the one below it to exist
building the page first means nothing real to read from
you cannot tell whether it works until the thing underneath exists
step.issues.title: Issues and the board
attest.issues.assigned.label: I assigned an issue to myself
attest.issues.in-progress.label: I moved it to In progress on the project board
attest.issues.commented.label: I commented on the issue saying how I plan to approach it
attest.issues.commented.hint: Even one sentence. It is the cheapest possible way to find out you misread the issue.
quiz.issues.stuck.prompt: You have been stuck on the same problem for two hours. What is the right move?
quiz.issues.stuck.option.a: Keep going — asking makes you look like you cannot do the job.
quiz.issues.stuck.option.b: Say where you are stuck: what you expected, what happened, what you have already tried.
quiz.issues.stuck.option.c: Move the issue back to To do and pick another one.
quiz.issues.stuck.option.d: Open a PR and let the reviewer work it out.
quiz.issues.stuck.explain: Two hours is roughly where a question stops being cheaper to avoid. Nobody is impressed by a silent week. Asking well is a skill in itself, and that three-part shape — expected, actual, tried — is most of it: it shows you did the work, and it lets someone help you in one reply instead of five.

check.database.emitted-again: The generated contract includes the relation
check.database.sandbox-branch: You are on your sandbox branch
check.database.model: `Product` is in the contract with the right fields
check.database.emitted: The generated contract is up to date
attest.database.dry-run-read.label: I read the `--dry-run` output before applying it
attest.database.dry-run-read.hint: Run `docker compose exec app npx prisma-cli db update --dry-run`. It prints what it would do and changes nothing. On a database with real customers in it, that is the difference between a change and an incident.
step.typescript.title: TypeScript, the parts you need
check.typescript.tsc-clean: The project type-checks, and your experiment is cleaned up
attest.typescript.saw-editor-error.label: I saw my editor mark the mistake before I ran anything
quiz.typescript.union-meaning.prompt: What does `string | null` mean when you see it on a field?
quiz.typescript.union-meaning.option.a: The field is a string that might be empty.
quiz.typescript.union-meaning.option.b: Either a string or nothing — and you must handle both.
quiz.typescript.union-meaning.option.c: The field is optional and can be left out.
quiz.typescript.union-meaning.option.d: It is a string that will be converted to null.
quiz.typescript.union-meaning.explain: The `|` means "one or the other". `content: string | null` says a post may genuinely have no content, and TypeScript will not let you call `.length` on it until you have checked which one you have. That check is the thing it is forcing you to remember.
ask.typescript.why-annotations.prompt: Your editor underlined the mistake before you ran anything. Nothing executed. How did it know?
ask.typescript.why-annotations.modelAnsw: Nothing ran. `createPost` says in its own signature that `title` is a string, so handing it a number contradicts something already written down. A contradiction is findable by reading the code, which needs no database, no server and no test run — that is why it is instant.
ask.typescript.why-annotations.lookFor.0: the function declares what type it takes
ask.typescript.why-annotations.lookFor.1: passing something else contradicts what is already written
ask.typescript.why-annotations.lookFor.2: a contradiction can be found by reading, without running
step.naming.title: What to call things
quiz.naming.file-case.prompt: You are adding a component that shows one product card. What do you call the file?
quiz.naming.file-case.explain: Files in this project are kebab-case — `posts-board.tsx`, `global-setup.ts`, `database-url.ts`. The component *inside* it is still `ProductCard`. Those two conventions are different on purpose, and the reason is dull but real: macOS and Windows treat `ProductCard.tsx` and `productcard.tsx` as the same file, Linux does not, and a repository that disagrees with itself about capitals breaks on somebody else’s machine.
quiz.naming.which-extension.prompt: Why is `posts-board.tsx` a `.tsx` while `route.ts` is a `.ts`?
quiz.naming.which-extension.option.a: `.tsx` is for files in the `app/` folder.
quiz.naming.which-extension.option.b: `.tsx` is for anything that runs in the browser.
quiz.naming.which-extension.option.c: `.tsx` is for files that contain JSX — HTML-shaped markup.
quiz.naming.which-extension.option.d: They are interchangeable; it is a matter of taste.
quiz.naming.which-extension.explain: The `x` is the only difference and it means "this file contains JSX". `route.ts` returns data and never writes a tag, so it does not need it. Put JSX in a `.ts` file and TypeScript reads the angle brackets as something else entirely and gives you an error that does not mention JSX at all.
quiz.naming.function-name.prompt: A function takes an unknown value and returns either a valid price or a reason it was refused. Best name?
quiz.naming.function-name.explain: A verb first, because it does something. `price` sounds like a value, not an action. `handle` is the emptiest verb in programming — it tells you nothing about what happens. And the last one describes the implementation, which will change; the name should survive that.
step.async.title: Nothing happens immediately
attest.async.saw-undefined.label: I deleted an `await` and read what came back instead
quiz.async.forgotten-await.prompt: You forget an `await` on a function that reads the database, then send the result as JSON. What does the caller receive?
quiz.async.forgotten-await.option.a: An error saying you forgot to await.
quiz.async.forgotten-await.option.c: `{}` — an empty object, with no error anywhere.
quiz.async.forgotten-await.explain: A promise has no properties of its own to serialise, so `JSON.stringify` on one produces `{}`. Nothing throws. This is the shape of bug that costs juniors whole afternoons: correct-looking code, a wrong answer, and nothing at all to read.
ask.async.what-async-returns.prompt: What do you actually get back when you call an `async` function, and what does `await` do to it?
ask.async.what-async-returns.modelAnswer: A promise — always, even when the body returns a plain number. A promise is a receipt: it stands for a value that is not here yet. `await` is what redeems the receipt for the thing itself, and it only works inside a function marked `async`, which is why the two words turn up together everywhere.
ask.async.what-async-returns.lookFor.0: you get a promise, not the value
ask.async.what-async-returns.lookFor.1: a promise is a receipt you can wait on
ask.async.what-async-returns.lookFor.2: `await` turns the receipt into the value
ask.async.what-async-returns.lookFor.3: `await` only works inside a function marked `async`
step.debugging.title: When it breaks
check.debugging.contract-restored: The contract and its generated files agree again
attest.debugging.found-in-logs.label: I found the real error in the container log, not in the browser
attest.debugging.read-the-diff.label: I read the assertion diff and it told me the answer
quiz.debugging.where-does-it-surface.pro: The browser shows `{"error":"Failed to list posts"}` and a 500. Where is the *real* error?
quiz.debugging.where-does-it-surface.opt: In the container log — the handler logged it before answering.
quiz.debugging.where-does-it-surface.exp: `internalError` calls `console.error(message, error)` and *then* answers with a flat message. That is deliberate — a raw error can contain table names, queries, sometimes connection strings, so the detail goes where your team can see it and the caller gets the summary. The detail always exists. You just have to know which window.
ask.debugging.first-question.prompt: Something worked an hour ago and does not now. What is the first question, and what command answers it?
ask.debugging.first-question.modelAnswer: What did I change? Almost always the answer is me, and `git diff` tells me in one second. It rules out every theory that starts "maybe Next.js is broken", and it costs nothing to ask. Restarting things sometimes fixes it and teaches me nothing, so I meet the same bug again next week.
ask.debugging.first-question.lookFor.2: it rules out a whole universe of other theories
step.what-tests-are.title: What a test actually is
attest.what-tests-are.saw-it-catch.label: I broke the ordering and watched a test fail and name it
quiz.what-tests-are.what-a-test-is.promp: What is a test, in one line?
quiz.what-tests-are.what-a-test-is.optio: A tool that finds bugs in your code automatically.
Code that sets up a situation, runs your code, and checks the answer is what you said it would be.
A check that your code compiles and has no syntax errors.
A report showing how much of your code has been run.
quiz.what-tests-are.what-a-test-is.expla: It is ordinary code, and it is not clever. It arranges a situation, calls your function, and compares what came back with what you claimed. A test cannot find a bug you never described — which is why the suite stayed green when the title limit broke.
ask.what-tests-are.what-tests-buy.prompt: Six months from now, someone changes a line near your endpoint. What have your tests bought them?
ask.what-tests-are.what-tests-buy.modelA: A fast answer to "did I break something somebody already decided mattered". That is not about catching bugs today — it is what makes the code editable at all. Code nobody dares touch is where projects die, and a suite that answers in thirty seconds is what lets a stranger change it. In six months that stranger is me.
ask.what-tests-are.what-tests-buy.lookFo: a fast answer to "did I break anything somebody wrote down"
it is what makes the code changeable at all
step.tdd.title: Write a test, then make it pass
check.tdd.sandbox-branch: You are on your sandbox branch
check.tdd.limit-restored: You put the title limit back to 200
check.tdd.no-route-yet: You have not written the route yet
check.tdd.runtime: The runtime is pinned to Node
check.tdd.order: The test was committed before the code
attest.tdd.green-but-broken.label: I saw the whole suite pass while the app was visibly broken
attest.tdd.green-but-broken.hint: That is the point of the experiment. Do not tick it until you have seen it.
quiz.tdd.envelope.prompt: Every handler in this project answers with `{ data }` or `{ error }`. What does that buy you?
quiz.tdd.envelope.option.b: Client code needs one way of reading a response, instead of a different shape per endpoint.
quiz.tdd.envelope.explain: Conventions like this are worth more than they look. Every consumer checks `response.ok`, then reads `body.data` or `body.error` — and that will be true of the endpoint you write next, without anyone having to ask.
ask.tdd.why-red-first.prompt: You just watched the whole suite pass while the app was broken. In your own words: why is it not enough for a test to pass?
ask.tdd.why-red-first.modelAnswer: A passing suite only tells me that the things somebody wrote tests for still work. Nobody had written a test for the title limit, so nothing noticed when I broke it. And a test I have only ever seen pass might not be testing anything at all — watching it fail first is how I know it is really connected.

ask.tdd.why-red-first.lookFor.1: nothing was watching the title limit
ask.tdd.why-red-first.lookFor.2: a test that has only ever passed might not be connected to the code

ask.post-happy.why-post-here.prompt: Back in the requests step you learned when to use POST instead of GET. Without looking: why is creating a post a POST?
ask.post-happy.why-post-here.modelAnswer: Because it changes something. A GET gets repeated — refresh, back button, a crawler following a link — and nothing asks me first. If creating a post were a GET, every one of those repeats would make another post. POST is the method for "this changes state", and the browser treats it accordingly.

quiz.post-validation.validation.prompt: Why does `POST /api/posts` look up the author before creating the post?
quiz.post-validation.validation.option.a: To warm up the database connection.
quiz.post-validation.validation.option.b: To copy the author name onto the post.
quiz.post-validation.validation.option.c: So a bad author id answers 422 with a clear message instead of an opaque database error.
quiz.post-validation.validation.option.d: It is left over and should be deleted.
quiz.post-validation.validation.explain: The database would reject it anyway — the foreign key sees to that. But the error would arrive as a constraint violation, get caught by the `catch`, and reach the caller as a generic 500. Checking first turns "something broke" into "this author does not exist".

ask.ui.client-again.prompt: You are about to add a page. Recall the rule from the Client Components step: how do you decide whether this file needs `'use client'`?
ask.ui.client-again.modelAnswer: I ask whether anything on it has to react after the page arrives — a click, typing, state that changes. attest.pull-request.reviewed-one.hint: A teammate’s, or one on any public repository you use — open source pull requests are public and readable. Read the description, then the tests, then the code, and ask one genuine question. Reviewing is half the job and it arrives in your first fortnight.
attest.pull-request.green-before-push.la: `npm test` and `npm run lint` both pass
attest.pull-request.green-before-push.hi: Run them before you push, not after somebody asks. Anything a machine can tell you in thirty seconds should never cost a reviewer a round trip. `npm run lint -- --fix` handles most of what the linter finds.

quiz.pull-request.review-feedback.prompt: A reviewer writes: "This works, but could it live in a plain function so it can be tested directly?" What are they doing?
quiz.pull-request.review-feedback.option: Proposing a change, and asking rather than telling because you may have context they lack.
Blocking the PR until you rewrite it.
quiz.pull-request.review-feedback.explai: Review comments are about the code, and a question is usually a real question. Two replies are both fine: "good idea, done", and "I tried that and it needs the request object — happy to change it if you still think so". What is not fine is resolving the thread without answering it.
ask.pull-request.history-recall.prompt: Your reviewer is about to read your commits. From the commit step, hours ago: what makes a history readable, and what makes one annoying to review?
ask.pull-request.history-recall.modelAns: Small commits that each do one thing, with subjects that say what changed rather than which file moved. A reviewer can read those one at a time and follow the reasoning. One enormous commit, or a run of "wip" and "fix stuff", makes them reconstruct my thinking from the diff — which is slow, and where review comments start to be about the wrong things.
one commit per one change, small and self-contained
the subject says what changed and why, not what file
a giant commit or "fix stuff" forces the reviewer to work it out
